why: The record of every hand edit to the DELE Spanish decks. Applied by spanish-fix.js; see that file's header for what an entry may carry and why the record exists at all. DELE A1 is being read one card at a time in Sep 2026, in batches of ten; this is what that pass has changed so far.

delea1.why: Folding the eight article cards into two and adding the three third-person object pronouns the generator's word list has no entry for changes what the deck holds, and a subtitle that goes on counting the old number is a claim the file itself refutes. The count was already wrong before any of this - the subtitle said 500 against 496 cards - so both figures are set to what is actually there. Both the 500 and the 490 pair are kept, so the chain still works on a deck freshly rebuilt from the generator. The figure was 493 for one commit, written when the plan was three inserted pronouns and left when it turned out to be two: les is a form on the le card rather than a card. A count in prose is wrong the moment the thing it counts moves, which is why check-claims.js exists one directory over — check it against the file rather than against the intention. It moved again when la tercera turned out to be a duplicate of tercero, tercera and was folded away: every count in the chain is kept so it still works on a deck freshly rebuilt from the generator.

delea1/de.why: The third bullet - 'used after the thing owned and before the owner' - was a usage NOTE standing in the list of translations, where the card renders it as though it were an English equivalent of the word. It moves into the gloss it qualifies. The list also left out three senses an A1 reader meets in the first week: origin (soy de Madrid), material (de madera) and topic (un libro de historia). Examples 2 and 3 were the same sentence with its two halves swapped - 'La esencia de las matematicas es la libertad' and 'La esencia de la libertad son las matematicas' - so the card showed one example twice; the second is dropped for a sentence that shows the origin sense.
senses: 's (after the thing owned, before the owner)
dropEx: La esencia de la libertad son las matemáticas.

delea1/que.why: Glossed as a conjunction only, so the RELATIVE PRONOUN - which is what its own first example shows, and one of the two commonest uses of the commonest word in Spanish - was missing. That example made the loss invisible: 'El color que me encanta es el rojo' was translated 'My favorite color is red', which translates the que away, so the card asked a reader to learn a word from a sentence whose English does not contain it. It is dropped for a sentence whose translation carries the relative through.
dropEx: El color que me encanta es el rojo.
ex: Este es el libro que me gusta.
This is the book that I like.

delea1/no.why: Glossed 'not' alone. The commonest English translation of Spanish no - no, in answer to a question - was missing, and the deck carries si as 'yes, yeah', so the pair was taught from one side only. The third example, 'No abrir antes de que pare el tren', is one of the deck's most reused sentences (it also illustrates de and que) and is an infinitive notice rather than everyday speech; it makes room for an answer.
dropEx: No abrir antes de que pare el tren.

delea1/la.why: THE DEFINITE ARTICLE, FOLDED FROM FOUR CARDS INTO ONE. el, la, los and las were four separate notes for one paradigm, which the deck's own stated policy already refuses everywhere else - a noun's plural sits beneath it and a feminine pair is taught as one card (el nino, la nina above los ninos, las ninas, 63 of them). Split, the four glosses had drifted apart: los was filed as a PRONOUN ('plural masculine or neuter pronoun') with 'the' missing altogether, though all three of its own examples used it as an article. Split, they also collided on the reverse card, where three of them prompted the reader with 'the' and nothing else. The surviving note keeps the lowest id of the four (u_delea1_4), which is the earliest and most frequent slot. The paradigm moves into Forms, where a paradigm belongs, and takes the el agua rule with it - which the deck was already illustrating on this card, in the example about oil and water, without saying anywhere what the reader was looking at. The third example, 'con los que charlar', uses los as a relative rather than as an article; it is dropped for one that shows the masculine plural plainly.
dropEx: Él no tiene amigos con los que charlar.
ex: Él trabaja todos los días excepto los domingos.
He works every day except Sundays.

delea1/un.why: THE INDEFINITE ARTICLE, FOLDED FROM FOUR CARDS INTO ONE, on the same reasoning as el, la above. Split, un/una/unos/unas had drifted the same way: una was filed as a PRONOUN meaning 'one' with 'a, an' missing, and unos and unas - the same word - were given opposite halves of its meaning, unos 'about, approximately' and unas 'some, a few', on two cards a hundred and fifty apart. The numeral uno keeps its own card. The four examples show all four forms and both senses, which three cannot, so maxEx is raised here and says why.
senses: unos, unas before a number — about, approximately
dropEx: Amar a alguien no es nunca un desperdicio.
ex: Él es un hombre de unos sesenta años.
He is around sixty years old.
Ella dijo unas palabras de agradecimiento por el regalo.
She said a few words of thanks for the present.

delea1/y.why: Two bullets, 'and' and 'plus, and', which is one gloss written twice - the second says nothing the first does not, and buries the arithmetic sense it was presumably meant to carry. The card is also the only place the deck can teach that y becomes e before a word beginning i- or hi- (madre e hija): there is no e card, and nothing else in the deck mentions it.

delea1/en.why: The gloss list left out the means-of-transport sense - which is exactly what the card's own first example is, 'Mejor te llevo hasta tu casa en coche'. The card showed a sentence for a meaning it did not list.

delea1/por.why: The weakest card of the first ten: glossed 'by' and 'for (indicates something given in an exchange)', while ALL THREE of its examples showed senses that were not on the list - por telefono (means), manana por la manana (time of day) and por que (why). The list now carries the senses an A1 reader meets, and por que gets a line of its own because the deck teaches the phrase nowhere else, though it uses it in examples on two cards. por and para both glossed to 'for', which on the English-to-Spanish card is one question with two right answers; both now carry a hint naming the other.

delea1/qué.why: Glossed 'what / which / what a / such'; 'such' is not a translation of que in any ordinary use and is dropped. Two of its three examples were por que, 'why' - a different item, which the deck lists separately in its own inventory of question words and which now has a line on the por card - so only one of the three taught the word on the card. They make room for the plain interrogative and the exclamative, the two uses the gloss claims.
dropEx: ¿Por qué no se lo dijiste a ella?
¿Por qué vas a visitar el Reino Unido?
ex: What a beautiful city this is!

delea1/me.why: Two of its three examples had English that does not contain the pronoun the card teaches - 'Se me ha ido el dolor de cabeza' rendered 'My headache has gone', and 'El color que me encanta es el rojo' rendered 'My favorite color is red', which is the same mistranslation that had to be dropped from the que card. A pronoun learnt from a sentence whose translation does not show it is not learnt. The first is also a dative of interest, a construction well above A1.
dropEx: Se me ha ido el dolor de cabeza.
El color que me encanta es el rojo.

delea1/se.why: The gloss was Wiktionary's own definition sentence - 'A reflexive or reciprocal pronoun: oneself, himself...' - which the card renders as though it were an English equivalent, and it carried only the reflexive. Three of the four things se does were missing, two of them illustrated elsewhere in this very deck: the impersonal and passive se (the qué card's example is '¿Qué idioma se habla en los Estados Unidos?') and the se that replaces le or les before lo and la (the por card's example is '¿Por qué no se lo dijiste a ella?'). The second example bolded saber, a different card's headword, and is dropped for one that shows the impersonal.
senses: one, you, people (impersonal and passive: se habla español)
to him, to her, to them (replacing le or les before lo, la, los, las)
dropEx: No podemos saber lo que va a ocurrir.

delea1/te.why: The first example is 'No quiero a otro. Te quiero a vos', which uses vos - the Rioplatense second person. This deck is built on the Instituto Cervantes' own Plan curricular and teaches tú, vosotros and os, so a single Rioplatense form standing in one example is a dialect the rest of the deck does not use. The reflexive sense was also missing, though te is the pronoun an A1 reader meets first in ¿cómo te llamas?
dropEx: No quiero a otro. Te quiero a vos.

delea1/con.why: The second bullet, 'Dependent preposition following certain verbs', is a usage note standing in the list of translations - the same fault as de's third bullet - and it displaced the sense it was presumably pointing at, con meaning 'to' after verbs of speaking (hablar con alguien). conmigo and contigo have no card anywhere in the deck and nothing else mentions them, so they go in Forms, which is where a paradigm belongs.
senses: to (after a verb of speaking: hablar con alguien)

delea1/para.why: Two bullets that overlapped almost completely - 'for, to (expressing a recipient)' and 'to, in order to, so, for' - and between them left out the deadline sense (para el lunes), the destination sense (salgo para Madrid), the concessive one (alto para su edad) and the point-of-view one, which is what the card's own first example is: 'Para muchas mujeres, el amor es lo primero', translated 'With many women, love always comes first'. Examples 2 and 3 showed the same sense as each other, so the third makes room for the purpose clause, which is the use that most distinguishes para from por.
senses: for, by (a deadline: para el lunes)
for, in the opinion of (para mí)
dropEx: Esa isla es un paraíso para los niños.
ex: Estudio español para viajar a México.
I'm studying Spanish in order to travel to Mexico.

delea1/mi.why: The gloss and the examples are right, and the one thing missing is the word standing one accent away from it: mí, the pronoun that follows a preposition (para mí), which has no card in the deck and is mentioned nowhere. It is not a form of mi, so the Forms label says what it actually is.
forms: with an accent, after a preposition

delea1/pero.why: Four glosses under one part of speech - 'but', 'well well', 'so', 'well (used for emphasis)' - of which the last three are the interjection, filed as a conjunction and written three ways. The second example, '¡No hay peros que valgan!', is the masculine NOUN un pero, an objection: a fourth sense the card did not list at all, in an idiom no A1 reader needs. The interjection keeps one line, the noun and its idiom go.
senses: but…, why… (opening an objection: ¡Pero qué dices!)
dropEx: ¡No hay peros que valgan!
ex: Quiero ir, pero no tengo tiempo.
I want to go, but I don't have time.

delea1/sí.why: The worst example-against-definition mismatch found so far: the card is glossed 'yes, yeah' and ALL THREE of its examples are a sí mismo - the prepositional reflexive pronoun, a different word that the card did not list. Nothing on the card taught the word it claims to teach. One of the three is kept under a sense that now names it, and the affirmative gets the two examples it never had, including the emphatic yo sí quiero, which is the use that makes sí more than a one-word answer.
senses: indeed, certainly (emphatic: yo sí quiero — I DO want to)
himself, herself, itself, oneself, themselves (after a preposition: a sí mismo)
dropEx: Creo que Tom se culpa a sí mismo.
Uno debería dar lo mejor de sí mismo.

delea1/si.why: The third bullet, 'points out a contradiction', is a usage note in the list of translations and describes a use without giving it - the protesting si of ¡Si yo no dije nada! It is replaced by the translation and the phrase that shows it.
senses: but (protesting: ¡Si yo no dije nada! — but I didn't say anything!)

delea1/bien.why: 'well (adverbial form of bueno)' and 'well' were the same gloss twice, the first carrying a note about bueno rather than a translation. Worse, none of the three examples taught the word: the first is the proverb 'No hay mal que por bien no venga', where bien is a NOUN; the second bolded bienes, the plural of that noun meaning goods; and the third bolded Mejor, which is bien's comparative and is the word that sentence actually teaches. The comparative has no card of its own, so it goes in Forms, and the three examples are replaced with the adverb.
dropEx: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
La Policía lleva casi un mes buscando los bienes robados.
Mejor te llevo hasta tu casa en coche.

delea1/eso.why: All three examples bolded Ésa, Éste and ése - three demonstratives, none of them eso, two of which are their own cards - so nothing on the card taught the word. They are also spelt with the accent the RAE dropped in 2010, and all three sat on the esto card as well, so two cards shared one wrong set of examples. Replaced, and the gloss now says what neuter means here: eso points at an idea or a situation rather than at a noun.
senses: that (neuter — an idea, a situation, or something not yet named)
dropEx: Ésa es la oficina en la que trabaja.
Éste es el mismo coche que tengo yo.
¿Es ése el tren que tengo que tomar?

delea1/esto.why: Glossed 'substitutes a noun one can't remember or can't remember the name of' - Wiktionary's entry for the hesitation filler, offered as the whole meaning of the word, so the card never said that esto means 'this'. Its three examples were the same three the eso card carried, bolding Ésa, Éste and ése, none of which is esto.
senses: this (neuter — an idea, a situation, or something not yet named)
dropEx: Ésa es la oficina en la que trabaja.
Éste es el mismo coche que tengo yo.
¿Es ése el tren que tengo que tomar?

delea1/caro, cara.why: 'dear (loved)' was given before 'expensive', which is the wrong way round - caro means expensive in ordinary use and 'dear' in the sense of loved is literary. Its third example bolded cara, the noun meaning face, in 'No me acuerdo de la cara de Tom' - a different word that only looks like the feminine of this one.
dropEx: No me acuerdo de la cara de Tom.

delea1/tú.why: One of six cards in this deck whose English gloss is 'you'. On the English-to-Spanish card the gloss is the whole of the front, so six cards were one question with six right answers. A group of that size is not hinted - naming five of the six on the front is worse than the ambiguity - so each is given a gloss that distinguishes it, which is the rule the Mandarin decks settled on. Its second and third examples bold ti and contigo, which are tú's own forms after a preposition and have no cards anywhere in the deck; they go in Forms so the examples are teaching something the card admits to.

delea1/usted.why: 'second person formal' is a grammatical description rather than a translation, and the card gave 'you (singular)' beside it, which does not distinguish it from tú. See the tú entry for the group this belongs to.

delea1/ustedes.why: Glossed 'you (plural), you guys, y'all, yous, yinz, ye' - five dialect forms of English carried straight out of Wiktionary, two of which (yinz, yous) are regional to a degree no learner of Spanish needs. What the card actually has to say is which Spanish-speaking places use it for whom. Two of its three examples were somebody else's card as well: one bolded les and one bolded usted, the singular.
senses: you (plural — formal in Spain, and the only plural you in Latin America)
dropEx: Daniel les dio las gracias a los policías.
¿Estaba Joe con usted ayer por la tarde?

delea1/vosotros.why: See the tú entry: one of six cards glossed 'you'. vosotros is Peninsular and informal, which is the whole of what tells it from ustedes.

delea1/os.why: See the tú entry. os is the object pronoun that goes with vosotros, so it is Peninsular too, and the card said neither.

delea1/el enero.why: THE TWELVE MONTHS WERE ALL HEADED WITH AN ARTICLE AND ALL GIVEN A PLURAL, AND SPANISH DOES NEITHER. The generator gives every noun its article and its plural beneath it, which is right for the 220 nouns it was written for and wrong for a month: one says en marzo, never en el marzo, and los marzos is not a form anyone uses. The days and the seasons are left alone, because there the article is real and so is the plural - el lunes is 'on Monday' and los lunes is 'on Mondays'.

delea1/el febrero.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el marzo.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural. Its second example was 'Tu vestido nuevo es la mar de bonito', where the matcher had bolded mar — the sea, inside an idiom that has nothing to do with the month.
dropEx: Tu vestido nuevo es la mar de bonito.

delea1/el abril.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural. Its second gloss, 'years of age', is the poetic plural (quince abriles) and is not A1.

delea1/el mayo.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural. Its second gloss, 'maypole', is a real but rare sense that has no place on an A1 card. Its second example was 'May a veces pasa el tiempo ella sola' — the English given name May, which the form matcher took for the Spanish month.
dropEx: May a veces pasa el tiempo ella sola.

delea1/el junio.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el julio.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el agosto.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el septiembre.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural. Its second example uses setiembre, the RAE's accepted variant spelling, which the card did not admit to having — so the sentence sat there with nothing marked in it. The variant goes in Forms.

delea1/el octubre.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el noviembre.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el diciembre.why: See the enero entry: a month takes no article and has no useful plural.

delea1/el jueves.why: Its second gloss was 'the letter J in the Spanish alphabet' - Wiktionary's entry for the radio-alphabet use of the word, which no reader of an A1 deck will ever meet. Thursday is the whole of it. The article and the plural stay: unlike a month, el jueves means 'on Thursday' and los jueves 'on Thursdays'.

delea1/el sábado.why: 'Saturday, Sabbath, sabbath' - the same word twice over in two capitalisations, and neither is what the card is for.

delea1/la primavera.why: Its second gloss, 'year of age', is the poetic plural (veinte primaveras) and is not A1.

delea1/su.why: The gloss is right and complete; what was missing is the plural sus, which the card's own second example bolds and which mi already carries in Forms. Two possessives in the same deck, one showing its plural and one not.

delea1/tu.why: Same as su: the plural tus is missing, though mi carries mis. tú, the pronoun one accent away, has a card of its own, so unlike mi/mí it needs no cross-reference here.

delea1/yo.why: The first bullet, 'first-person singular pronoun in the nominative case', is a grammatical description standing where a translation goes. The card also said nothing about the one fact an English speaker most needs: Spanish normally leaves the subject pronoun out, and using yo is emphatic or contrastive - which is why two of the three examples are 'que yo' after a comparison rather than a plain subject. Examples 2 and 3 were the same construction twice, so one makes room for the plain subject the card never showed.
senses: me (after que or como: más viejo que yo)
dropEx: Él es el doble de viejo que yo.

delea1/más.why: 'more / -er / most / -est' covers the comparative and the superlative and leaves out the two other things más does: no… más and nunca más, 'not any more', which is what the card's own third example shows, and the plus of arithmetic. None of the three examples was the plain comparative - the first is más o menos, a set phrase meaning roughly - so one is replaced with it.
senses: any more, any longer (with no or nunca)
dropEx: Él tiene más o menos tu misma edad.
ex: Este libro es más interesante que el otro.
This book is more interesting than the other one.

delea1/todo.why: Headed todo alone while two of its three examples bolded todas and todos, so the card showed forms its headword did not admit to having - which is exactly what the deck's own convention exists to prevent (bueno, buena above buenos, buenas). It is also glossed as a determiner only, and todo as a PRONOUN meaning 'everything' is a different thing a reader meets just as early. The first example, 'todo el mundo', is a set phrase already carried on other cards, so it makes room for the pronoun.
dropEx: A todo el mundo le gusta la música.

delea1/ya.why: 'already' was missing, and it is the commonest translation of ya by a long way - the card's own third example, 'Ella ya había estado en Inglaterra', is that sense, and its English ('She has been to England once') drops the word entirely. What the card gave instead was 'now', 'right now' and 'indicates completion of an action', the last being a usage note rather than a translation. All three examples go: the first is the headache sentence a third card was already using, the second uses 'se me hace que', which is Mexican colloquial, and the third is the mistranslation.
dropEx: Ya se me quitó el dolor de cabeza.
Se me hace que ya nos hemos conocido.
Ella ya había estado en Inglaterra una vez.
ex: I don't live here any more.

delea1/ahora.why: The second gloss, 'just now, just a moment ago (in the past)', is a regional use that reads on an A1 card as though ahora ordinarily referred to the past, which it does not. It is replaced by the two phrases a reader really meets, ahora mismo and por ahora.
senses: for now, for the time being (por ahora)

delea1/muy.why: Its second example bolded mucho, which is another card - and it is not an accident of the generator's form matching but the single commonest mistake an English speaker makes in Spanish, since both answer to 'very much'. muy goes before an adjective or an adverb and mucho everywhere else, and neither card said so. The rule goes in Forms, where it can be read at a glance, and the example is replaced with one that shows muy doing its own job.
forms: before a noun or a verb, use
dropEx: Él tiene mucho dinero, pero casi ningún amigo.

delea1/mucho.why: The other half of the muy entry above: mucho is glossed as a determiner alone, though it is just as often the adverb that follows a verb (trabaja mucho), which is the use that gets confused with muy. Its third example is 'Mucha gente rica vive en este barrio', and mucha was not in the Forms at all, so after the rebold that sentence stood with nothing marked in it — which reads exactly like a sentence the deck chose and then forgot to point at.
senses: a lot, very much (after a verb: trabaja mucho)
forms: before an adjective or an adverb, use

delea1/aquí.why: Nothing wrong with the gloss; the card simply did not say where aquí sits among the four words this deck teaches for here and there. ahí, allí and allá all have cards of their own, so the distinction is worth one line.

delea1/algo.why: The pronoun is right; algo as an ADVERB - 'a bit, somewhat', as in es algo caro - was missing, and it is the sense a reader meets as soon as they start describing things. The first example is Lacan's definition of love, which is abstract enough that a reader can follow the Spanish and still not know what algo does in it.
dropEx: Amar es dar algo que no se tiene.
ex: This book is a bit expensive.

delea1/bueno, buena.why: Two bullets that both read 'good', and neither of the two things a reader most needs: that bueno shortens to BUEN before a masculine noun (un buen día), which has no card and is mentioned nowhere in the deck, and that bueno on its own is the everyday filler for 'well…' or 'all right'. Its comparative mejor likewise has no card - it is already in bien's Forms and belongs here too.

delea1/él.why: Two of its three examples were another word: the first bolded ello, the neuter pronoun, which has no card in this deck, and the third bolded ella, which has one. What was missing from the gloss is that él is also what follows a preposition (para él) - Spanish has no separate object form - and that it is one accent away from the article el, which after the article fold is the very next card but one.
dropEx: No soy un artista. Nunca tuve mente para ello.
A ella le comenzó a gustar esa casa.

delea1/ella.why: Two of its three examples bolded él and Ellos, both of them cards of their own, so only one of the three taught the word. The gloss also carried a grammatical description - 'used subjectively and after prepositions to refer to feminine nouns' - where a translation goes, and the plural ellas had no card and no mention.
dropEx: Seguramente él me llamará por teléfono esta noche.
Ellos lo oyeron bajar por las escaleras.

delea1/ellos.why: Two of its three examples bolded les, which is now a form on the le card and was nowhere at all when these were chosen. The feminine ellas has no card and was not mentioned. And the deck carried a SEPARATE card for ellas, the feminine plural, which is a form rather than a word of its own — nosotras has no card, so this was inconsistent with its own sibling as well as a duplicate of the Forms row added here. Fourth duplicate found, after la tercera, padres and this one. The card is headed as a pair now, which is the deck's convention for exactly this shape. maxEx is 4 here for the reason un, una's is: a card teaching two forms needs an example of each, and the feminine one would not otherwise fit.
senses: ellos — they (men, or a mixed group)
dropEx: Daniel les dio las gracias a los policías.
A los gatos no les gusta el agua.

delea1/nosotros.why: Glossed 'we (masculine plural)' and 'ourselves', of which the second is nos rather than nosotros. The feminine nosotras, which the second example bolds, had no mention.

delea1/nos.why: The reflexive and reciprocal sense was missing, though the second example is one ('ya nos hemos conocido' — we have met each other before).

delea1/nada.why: 'nothing, zero, zilch, not...anything' - zilch is slang, and zero is wrong, nada not being the number. What it left out is the ADVERB, 'not at all', which is what BOTH of the first two examples show (no le gusta salir para nada, no estás para nada de acuerdo) - so two of three sentences illustrated a sense the card did not carry. The double negative goes in Forms: a Spanish sentence keeps its no when nada follows the verb, which is the rule an English speaker breaks first.
senses: anything (after a negative: no veo nada)

delea1/cómo.why: 'how?' alone. Missing the two uses a reader meets first after it: ¿cómo es? for what something is like, and cómo on its own as 'sorry?' when asking for something to be repeated.

delea1/este.why: A FAMILY WITH NO FORMS AT ALL WHILE ITS EXAMPLES BOLD THE INFLECTIONS. The deck's own convention is an adjective headed with its feminine and its plural beneath it (bueno, buena above buenos, buenas), and the demonstratives and quantifiers were left out of it - so este was headed este while its examples bolded estos, and one of them bolded ese, which is a card of its own. Every card in the family is brought into the convention at once: doing one of eight would leave the deck disagreeing with itself about how a determiner is written. este also gets the pronoun use ('this one'), which since the RAE dropped the accent in 2010 is spelt exactly like the determiner.
dropEx: También me gusta la voz de ese cantante.

delea1/ese.why: See the este entry: the same family, the same fault. Two of its three examples bolded estos and este, which are the neighbouring card.
dropEx: La experiencia lo dice todo en estos casos.
La vida de este paciente está en peligro.

delea1/aquel.why: See the este entry. Two of its three examples bolded esta and esa, both of them other cards.
senses: that (over there, further off than ese)
dropEx: Seguramente él me llamará por teléfono esta noche.
A ella le comenzó a gustar esa casa.
ex: That building over there is very old.
En aquella época no había teléfonos.
In those days there were no telephones.

delea1/poco.why: See the este entry: no Forms, while two of its three examples bold pocos and pocas. The adverb (dormí poco) was missing too, and so was un poco, which is what the first example actually shows.

delea1/otro.why: See the este entry: no Forms, while two of its three examples bold otra and otros. Note also that otro takes no article in Spanish - one says otro café, never un otro café - which is the mistake an English speaker makes first.

delea1/mal.why: All three of its examples were a different word: the first two are the masculine NOUN el mal (evil, harm) and its plural males, and the third bolds malo, which is a card of its own. Nothing on the card taught the adverb it is for.
dropEx: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
El dinero es la raíz de todos los males.
Eres más lento que el caballo del malo.

delea1/malo, mala.why: The mirror of bueno: malo shortens to MAL before a masculine noun (un mal día), which is why the adverb card and this one look alike, and its comparative is peor. Neither had a card or a mention. 'bad, evil, mean' is also three words for one sense.

delea1/o.why: Its second example was 'Tus oes parecen aes' - your o's look like a's - which is the plural of the LETTER o, on a card about the conjunction. And o becomes U before a word beginning o- or ho- (siete u ocho), exactly as y becomes e, with no u card anywhere in the deck to say so.
dropEx: Tus oes parecen aes.

delea1/ser.why: ser and estar both glossed 'to be' and neither said a word about which is which, though telling them apart is the single defining problem of A1 Spanish. The gloss gestured at it - 'to be (essentially or identified as)' - in language a beginner cannot act on; it is replaced by the list of things ser is actually used for, and the rule goes in Forms on both cards. They also collided on the English-to-Spanish card, where 'to be' was one question with two right answers, so both now carry a line naming the other. The third example is the reversed twin of a sentence the de card was showing.
senses: to be — identity, origin, profession, time, possession, material
to be (forming the passive: fue construido en 1920)
forms: for a state or a place, use
dropEx: La esencia de la libertad son las matemáticas.

delea1/estar.why: The other half of the ser entry. Glossed as location and presence only - 'to be (have a temporary or permanent location in space)' - which leaves out the sense the ser/estar question actually turns on, a STATE or a condition: estoy cansado, la sopa está fría. The second and third examples are both that sense, so the card was showing what it did not say.
senses: to be — a state or a condition (estoy cansado)
to be — a place (está en Madrid)
to be (forming the continuous: está lloviendo)

delea1/el aeropuerto.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. This is the worst of them: the second gloss on the AIRPORT card was 'a Peruvian dish based on fried rice with chicken eggs and various other ingredients'.

delea1/la planta.why: Glossed with a botanical definition that runs off the end of its own sentence - 'plant or of the Chlorophyta, a eukaryote that includes double-membraned chloroplasts in its' - and it left out the sense the card's OWN THIRD EXAMPLE uses: planta is a floor or storey of a building (viven en la planta doce). The sole of the foot goes with it, since that is the other everyday sense.
senses: floor, storey (la planta baja — the ground floor)

delea1/la policía.why: Glossed 'Civility, polity, public order, police, fineness, neatness, urbanity' - an eighteenth-century dictionary's sense list, capitalised, with the modern meaning fourth of seven. What the card actually has to teach is the pair its own examples show without explaining: la policía is the FORCE and el policía is one officer.
senses: el policía, la policía — a police officer

delea1/difícil.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. Nine synonyms for one word: 'difficult, hard, tough, challenging, rough, tricky, trying, arduous, testing'.

delea1/la televisión.why: 'television' and then 'television set, TV set, television receiver, television, telly' - five names for the box, one of them repeating the gloss above it.

delea1/la gente.why: 'guys, lads (used to address a group of people)' is a vocative that Spanish barely has, and the card left out the one thing about gente that an English speaker gets wrong every time: it is grammatically SINGULAR, which its own first example shows (la gente está de acuerdo) without saying so. The plural gentes, which the second example bolds, is literary.
dropEx: La plaza está abarrotada de gentes.
ex: Mucha gente vive en la ciudad.
A lot of people live in the city.

delea1/aún.why: The third gloss trailed a description - 'even (implying an extreme example in the case mentioned)'. And aun without the accent is a different word meaning 'even', which has no card; the two are one accent apart and the accent is the whole distinction.

delea1/deber.why: The modal sense a reader needs was MISSING: deber is 'must, should', which is what the card's own first example is (debería seguir los consejos). What it gave instead was 'to owe' and then deber DE, the guessing sense, described rather than translated. Its third example bolds deberes, the masculine noun meaning homework - a fourth thing the card did not list.
senses: deber de — must, probably (a guess: debe de estar en casa)

delea1/tampoco.why: Its gloss list was broken by the extractor: 'either (as well' and 'with implied negative)' are two halves of one parenthesis, split at the comma inside it and rendered as two separate translations.

delea1/querer.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. 'to desire, to want, to want to, to love, to be fond of' is two senses written five times. It also left out querer decir, which is how Spanish says 'to mean'.

delea1/antes.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. Five glosses for one word. antes de, which is how it is nearly always used, was not among them.
senses: antes de — before (a time or an action)

delea1/mismo, misma.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. 'same, identical, one and the same, similar, alike' - and 'similar' is not what mismo means. The emphatic use (yo mismo, hoy mismo) was missing.
senses: right, very (hoy mismo — this very day)

delea1/volver.why: FOUND BY A PROBE FOR A BOLDED WORD THAT IS NOT A FORM OF ITS HEADWORD. examples.py matches a sentence on any inflected form, and the match is not always a word: nine sentences across the deck illustrate a word that merely SHARES LETTERS with the card's, or a related noun that is not a form of the verb at all. Every one renders perfectly - a real sentence, a real translation, a bolded word - and teaches something else. Its third example is 'da la vuelta a la página', which is the noun la vuelta rather than a form of the verb.
senses: to return, to come back, to go back
volver a + infinitive — to do something again (vuelvo a leerlo)
dropEx: Por favor da la vuelta a la página.
ex: Vuelvo a casa a las seis.

delea1/entrar.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. Five ways of saying 'to go in'. Note that Spanish says entrar EN (or entrar a in Latin America), never entrar without a preposition.
senses: to go in, to come in, to enter

delea1/el salón.why: A SWEEP FOR GLOSSES CARRIED STRAIGHT OUT OF WIKTIONARY. Measured over the whole deck: nineteen glosses are a grammatical description, an antiquarian sense or a run of synonyms rather than an English equivalent a reader can use. They are fixed together, because the fault is one fault - the extractor takes a dictionary entry's whole sense list, and a dictionary is written for someone who already knows the word. 'living room, sitting room, parlor, drawing room, hall (meeting hall)' - four names for one room, two of them dated.

delea1/quién.why: 'if only' and 'I wish' are the exclamative ¡Quién pudiera!, which is not A1, and '(with de) whose?' was written as a note rather than as the phrase. The plural quiénes, which the card's own second example bolds, was in no Forms row.

delea1/el señor, la señora.why: 'mister, sir, lord, Ms, a title or form of address for a woman' - a mixed list in which the masculine and the feminine senses are shuffled together and the last entry is a description rather than a translation. The card is a pair, so the glosses are given as a pair.

delea1/hacer.why: 'to do, perform, execute, carry out' is four words for one sense, and the two uses of hacer that an A1 course teaches on its first day were both missing: the weather (hace frío, hace calor) and hace + a length of time for 'ago'. The deck notices the first without saying it - the tiempo card's own example is about complaining of the weather. The second example is a subjunctive (que nos hagan), which is well above this level.
senses: hace frío, hace calor — it is cold, it is hot
hace dos años — two years ago
dropEx: Vamos a pedir que nos hagan una foto.

delea1/porque.why: The gloss is right; what the card could not say is the thing readers actually get wrong, that the question is TWO WORDS with an accent. por qué now has a line on the por card, and this is the other half of it. Two of its three examples were also the same sentence with a different second half.
dropEx: Me quedé dormido porque mi alarma no sonó.
ex: I'm not going out because it's raining.

delea1/la casa.why: Glossed 'house' alone, though TWO of its three examples mean home rather than house - quedarse en casa, llevarte hasta tu casa - and en casa and a casa drop the article, which is the form a reader meets first.
senses: home (en casa — at home, a casa — home)

delea1/el tiempo.why: Glossed 'time' and then four synonyms for a length of time - and WEATHER was missing, though the card's own third example is 'la gente se queja a menudo del tiempo', translated 'people often complain about the weather'. The card was showing a sense it did not carry.
senses: a while, a length of time

delea1/dos.why: Two of its three examples are 'ninguno de los dos' and 'ninguna de las dos' - los dos meaning both, which the card did not list.

delea1/nunca.why: Like nada, nunca keeps the no when it follows the verb - which the card's own first example shows (no es nunca un desperdicio) and did not say.

delea1/dónde.why: Its unaccented half, donde, now has a card, so this one names it — the same pairing cómo/como and cuándo/cuando now have.

delea1/decir.why: 'to pronounce' and 'sound out' are not what decir means - that is pronunciar - and es decir, which is how Spanish says 'that is to say', was missing.
senses: es decir — that is to say

delea1/también.why: 'also, too, as well, so' - three ways of saying one thing and then 'so', which también does not mean. The echo it is most often used in, yo también, is the mirror of the yo tampoco now on the tampoco card, and neither said so.
senses: yo también — me too, so do I

delea1/sobre.why: Five prepositions for 'on' and then 'about' - and the card's own second example is 'Quisiera algunos sobres', I'd like some envelopes, which is the masculine NOUN el sobre, a sense the card did not carry at all. The time sense (sobre las tres, around three) was missing too, and it is the one an A1 reader needs to arrange to meet someone.
senses: around, about (a time: sobre las tres)

delea1/sin.why: The gloss is right and left out the commonest shape the word takes: sin before an infinitive, 'without …-ing'. Its second example is a subjunctive (sin que yo lo sepa) translated with 'unbeknownst', which is neither A1 Spanish nor A1 English.
dropEx: Lo ha hecho sin que yo lo sepa.

delea1/ver.why: Four glosses for 'to see' - and 'to watch', which is what BOTH of the first two examples are (ver la televisión, viendo la tele), was not among them. The card was showing a sense it did not carry, twice.

delea1/el hombre.why: 'man (adult male human)' and 'man' are the same gloss twice, the first carrying a dictionary's disambiguation. What the two bullets should have been is the individual and the generic - el mejor amigo del hombre, which is the card's own first example, is mankind rather than a man.

delea1/alguien.why: Two pairs of synonyms for one word. What is worth a line instead is that alguien is invariable - no feminine, no plural - and that as an object it takes the personal a, which all three of the card's examples do without saying so.
forms: invariable; as an object takes a

delea1/siempre.why: 'in spite of it' and 'still...at least' are regional idioms carried out of a dictionary, and the second is not English. What a reader needs instead is para siempre and siempre que, neither of which has a home anywhere else in the deck.
senses: siempre que — whenever, as long as

delea1/hasta.why: THE WORST CARD OF THE BATCH: hasta was filed as an ADVERB meaning 'even', and all three of its examples are the preposition meaning 'until' or 'as far as' (hasta tu casa, llegó hasta los 30 grados, desde la mañana hasta la noche). The part of speech was wrong, the one gloss was a marginal sense, and nothing on the card taught what every sentence on it was doing. ¡Hasta luego! goes with it: it is the first thing an A1 reader ever says in Spanish and the deck had it nowhere.
senses: up to, as far as (a place)
even (hasta yo lo sé — even I know that)

delea1/ahí.why: 'that (in certain phrases)' is a description of a use rather than a translation. ahí is the middle of a set of three - aquí, ahí, allí - and where it sits among them is the whole of what tells it from the other two; aquí already carries the cross-reference and this is its other half. por ahí, which the second example shows, was not listed.

delea1/ir.why: One gloss, and it was a description - 'to go (away from speaker and listener)'. Missing were the two things ir is most used for and which an A1 course reaches in its first fortnight: ir a + infinitive, which is how Spanish makes the everyday future, and irse, to leave. The card's own third example bolds Vamos, which is neither of the senses it listed.
senses: ir a + infinitive — to be going to (voy a comer — I'm going to eat)
irse — to leave, to go away

delea1/el día.why: Two glosses, 'day (any period of 24 hours)' and 'day (a period from midnight to the following midnight)', which are a dictionary telling one sense from another the reader will never need to tell apart. What is missing is buenos días — the first thing said in a Spanish lesson — and todos los días, which is the card's own second example. día is also masculine although it ends in -a, which is the trap every English speaker falls into, and the card said so only in the small part-of-speech line.
senses: de día — by day, in the daytime

delea1/uno.why: Two of its three examples were the indefinite ARTICLE, bolding una and unos - both now forms on the un, una card - and the third is broken Spanish: 'Este coche el igual que uno nuevo' has el where es belongs. So one example taught the wrong word twice and the other did not parse. All three are replaced. uno as the impersonal pronoun (uno nunca sabe) was missing too.
forms: before a masculine noun it shortens
dropEx: Todo el mundo se merece una segunda oportunidad.
Este coche el igual que uno nuevo.
Por favor toma un descanso por unos días.
ex: Uno de mis amigos vive en Madrid.
One of my friends lives in Madrid.

delea1/la noche.why: Two disambiguated glosses and none of the three phrases the word is actually met in: buenas noches, esta noche - which is the card's own first example, translated 'tonight' - and por la noche.
senses: buenas noches — good evening, good night

delea1/el acuerdo.why: Glossed as the noun alone, though TWO of its three examples are estar de acuerdo, which is how Spanish says 'to agree' and is a phrase rather than a use of the noun. 'compromise' is also not what acuerdo means - that is un compromiso, or in the English sense una concesión.

delea1/el trabajo.why: The gloss is right and thin: trabajo is also a single piece of work - an essay, an assignment - which is the sense a student meets first. The verb it is built on has a card of its own and neither pointed at the other.
senses: a piece of work, an assignment

delea1/el padre, la madre.why: 'father, parent, mother' - and 'parent' is not what padre means on its own. It is what the MASCULINE PLURAL means: los padres is 'the parents', covering both, which is one of the first facts about Spanish gender a reader needs and which the card had folded into the middle of a list as though it were a third translation of the singular. The deck also carried a SECOND card headed 'padres' — a bare plural, filed as 'noun' with no gender, glossed 'parents'. That is the veces fault again (a plural standing as a headword) and a duplicate of the sense block above, so it is folded away. Its three examples were all about somebody's parents and are covered here.

delea1/nadie.why: 'nobody (anyone or anybody)' is a parenthetical description rather than a translation. The card also had only TWO examples where every other card in the deck has three, and it said nothing about the two rules that govern the word: the no stays when nadie follows the verb, and as an object it takes the personal a - which its own first example does.
senses: anybody (after a negative: no veo a nadie)

delea1/hablar.why: Two synonyms, a definition ('to communicate using words') and a disambiguation. Its third example is also broken Spanish - 'al menos que le hablen' should be a menos que - so it is replaced by the question a reader will be asked in their first conversation.
dropEx: Él nunca habla al menos que le hablen.

delea1/después.why: 'later, afterwards, afterward, post' is one gloss written twice over in two spellings plus 'post', which is not English for this. And después DE, which is what all three of the card's examples are, was not listed at all.

delea1/desde.why: The glosses are right and carry a dictionary's parentheses where the phrase would serve better. desde hace, which is how Spanish says how long something has been going on, was missing and has no other home in the deck.
senses: desde hace — for (a length of time up to now: desde hace dos años)

delea1/el dinero.why: 'wealth' is la riqueza, not dinero. And the Forms row gave a plural, los dineros, which is archaic and jocular - the same fault as the twelve months, the generator handing every noun a plural whether or not the word has a useful one. Cleared rather than corrected: a card that shows a form nobody uses is teaching it.

delea1/claro, clara.why: The card's third example is 'Bate las claras del huevo', which is the feminine NOUN la clara, an egg white - a sense the card did not list, so the sentence sat there illustrating nothing on it. And ¡claro!, which is among the commonest words in spoken Spanish, was missing.

delea1/el momento.why: 'timing' is not what momento means. What the card needed instead is the two phrases it is nearly always met in, one of which is its own first example (por el momento).
senses: por el momento, de momento — for the moment

delea1/tener.why: 'to be (a condition or quality)' is a description standing in for the single most important pattern in A1 Spanish: tener hambre, sed, frío, calor, sueño, miedo, and tener … años for someone's age - where English uses 'to be'. The card's own third example is tener miedo, so it was showing the pattern without naming it. tener QUE, which is how Spanish says 'have to', was missing as well.
senses: tener que + infinitive — to have to (tengo que ir)
tener hambre, sed, frío, calor, sueño, miedo — to be hungry, thirsty, cold, hot, sleepy, afraid
tener … años — to be … years old

delea1/el estado.why: 'country, land (any broad area or territory)' is a dictionary's paraphrase and is not the sense TWO of the card's three examples use: estado de ánimo is a mood and el estado de mi amigo is his condition. State as a condition was missing from a card two thirds of whose sentences are that sense.
senses: state (a country, or a region of one)

delea1/mañana.why: Filed as an ADVERB meaning tomorrow, while TWO of its three examples are the feminine NOUN la mañana, the morning (por la mañana, todas las mañanas, de la mañana). The card was one part of speech and its sentences were mostly the other. 'soon' and 'shortly' are pronto, which has a card of its own.
senses: por la mañana — in the morning
pasado mañana — the day after tomorrow

delea1/el lugar.why: 'place' alone, and the card's own first example is en primer lugar, which is a phrase rather than that sense. en lugar de, which is how Spanish says 'instead of', has no other home in the deck.
senses: en primer lugar — in the first place, first

delea1/nuevo, nueva.why: 'new, brand new, all-new' is one gloss written three times, and de nuevo - which is what the card's FIRST example is ('nunca regresó a la escuela de nuevo') - was not among them.

delea1/el hijo, la hija.why: Glossed 'son' and 'child (of unknown gender)' - so DAUGHTER was missing from a card that is a pair and whose second example is hija. los hijos for children of both sexes is the same masculine-plural rule as los padres, and gets the same treatment.
senses: los hijos — children (sons and daughters together)

delea1/allí.why: A description rather than a translation, and no mention of where allí sits among aquí, ahí and allá - which is the whole of what tells the four apart and which aquí and ahí now both carry.
senses: there (away from both the speaker and the listener)

delea1/menos.why: 'less, least' and nothing else - so menos … que, the comparative of inferiority, was missing, and so were al menos and por lo menos, and the minus of arithmetic. Its third example is the same broken sentence the hablar card carried, 'al menos que le hablen' for a menos que.
senses: al menos, por lo menos — at least
dropEx: Él nunca habla al menos que le hablen.
ex: Hoy hace menos frío que ayer.
It's less cold today than yesterday.

delea1/el amigo, la amiga.why: Glossed 'friend' once for a card that teaches a pair, and silent on the masculine plural covering a mixed group - the third card in this deck with that fact to state, after los padres and los hijos, and the third time it was missing.
senses: los amigos — friends (of either sex together)

delea1/nuestro.why: Glossed 'ours' - the pronoun - while TWO of its three examples are the possessive DETERMINER, 'our' (Nuestra escuela, Nuestros planes). The card's main sense was missing and it had no Forms at all, though both of those examples bold an inflection.

delea1/la mujer.why: Right as far as it goes; worth saying that the 'wife' sense competes with la esposa, which has no card, so a reader meeting mujer for wife has no way to place it.

delea1/hoy.why: 'today, tonight (on the current day)' - hoy does not mean tonight; that is esta noche, which now sits on the noche card. hoy en día was missing.
senses: hoy en día — nowadays, these days

delea1/tres.why: Right, and thin: the card's own third example is 'a las tres de la tarde', telling the time, which is the shape a reader meets a number in before they meet it counting.

delea1/haber.why: 'have' and 'forms the perfect aspect' - a description, and between them they left out HAY, which is 'there is' and 'there are' and is what the card's own third example is ('No hay nada tan importante como el tiempo'). It is the most useful thing about the verb and the card did not carry it. hay que goes with it. hay is not in the card's own conjugation table - it is the impersonal form, which no person-and-number grid has a row for - so after the rebold its example stood with nothing marked in it. It goes in Forms, where it is worth stating anyway.
senses: to have (forming the perfect: he comido — I have eaten)
hay que + infinitive — one must, it is necessary to

delea1/el nombre.why: 'name' and 'noun', the second being the grammarian's sense, offered before the distinction a reader actually needs: el nombre is the first name and the surname is el apellido, which has no card in the deck at all.
senses: first name (the surname is el apellido)

delea1/mío.why: Two examples where every other card has three, no Forms though its second example bolds mías, and only the pronoun - un amigo mío, the stressed possessive standing after its noun, is the other half of the word and was not there.
senses: of mine, my own (after the noun: un amigo mío)
ex: Un amigo mío vive en Sevilla.
A friend of mine lives in Seville.

delea1/saber.why: saber and conocer both gloss to 'to know', which on the English-to-Spanish card is one question with two right answers, and neither said which is which - the second classic A1 confusion after ser and estar. saber is a fact or a skill, conocer a person or a place; both now carry the rule in Forms and name the other on the reverse card. 'to understand (a fact)' and 'to know how to do something' were descriptions rather than translations.
senses: saber + infinitive — to know how to (sabe nadar)
forms: for a person or a place, use

delea1/conocer.why: The other half of the saber entry: four glosses, all of them 'to know' in some wording, and nothing about the division between the two verbs.
senses: to know (a person or a place), to be familiar with
forms: for a fact or a skill, use

delea1/el radio.why: FOUND BY A PROBE RATHER THAN BY READING: every Forms plural in the deck was checked against every example sentence in it, and 79 plurals appear nowhere. Most of that is noise - a feminine plural of an adjective has no reason to turn up - but it surfaced a handful of forms that are not Spanish. This one is the worst: el radio is the RADIUS, or the metal radium. The radio set is LA radio, feminine, which is what all three of the card's examples use - so the headword was the wrong word and the gender line was wrong with it. The plural was written 'los/las radios', a slash the generator emits for a noun it thinks takes either gender.

delea1/el internet.why: FOUND BY A PROBE RATHER THAN BY READING: every Forms plural in the deck was checked against every example sentence in it, and 79 plurals appear nowhere. Most of that is noise - a feminine plural of an adjective has no reason to turn up - but it surfaced a handful of forms that are not Spanish. Its plural was 'los/las internets'.
senses: the internet (usually with no article: en internet)

delea1/el mar.why: FOUND BY A PROBE RATHER THAN BY READING: every Forms plural in the deck was checked against every example sentence in it, and 79 plurals appear nowhere. Most of that is noise - a feminine plural of an adjective has no reason to turn up - but it surfaced a handful of forms that are not Spanish. Its plural was written 'los/las mares'. The feminine la mar is real but poetic and survives mainly in set phrases, which is where the card's own second example uses it (la mar de bonito, 'ever so pretty').
senses: la mar — the sea (poetic); la mar de — ever so, loads of

delea1/veces.why: THE WORST HEADWORD IN THE DECK SO FAR: the card was headed veces - a PLURAL - and filed as a PREPOSITION glossed 'by' and 'times (multiplication)'. The word is la vez, a feminine noun meaning a time or an occasion, and all three of the card's examples are that noun in one of its phrases: a veces, dos veces, algunas veces. delea1/serio, seria.why: Seven synonyms in two disambiguated blocks - 'serious, earnest, sober, solemn (without humor)' and 'serious, grave, deep (important, weighty)'. en serio, which is what the card's own first example is, was not among them.

delea1/la tarde.why: Its third example is 'Él llega tarde a la escuela', which is the ADVERB tarde meaning late - a different word from the noun the card teaches, and one it did not list. buenas tardes and por la tarde were missing as well, which are the two shapes the noun is met in.

delea1/la hora.why: 'hour (a time period of sixty minutes)' and 'time', and neither of the two questions the word exists for: ¿qué hora es? and ¿a qué hora…?, the second being the card's own third example.

delea1/demasiado, demasiada.why: Filed as an adjective, and the card's FIRST example is the adverb - 'La vida es demasiado corta', life is too short - which is a use it did not list. delea1/entre.why: All three examples were the SAME SENTENCE three times over - 'X es muy popular entre Y', with X and Y swapped - so the card asked one thing thrice and taught it once. That is the worst example duplication found in the deck. 'from' is also not a meaning of entre.

delea1/la familia.why: 'family (group of people related to each other)' and 'family' are the same gloss twice, the first carrying a dictionary's definition.

delea1/la cuenta.why: A COMPLETE MISS: glossed 'count, tally, operation', and not one of those three appears anywhere on the card, while ALL THREE of its examples are senses it does not list - darse cuenta de (to realise), a fin de cuentas, and pagar la cuenta, the bill. delea1/todavía.why: 'even' is incluso, or aún; todavía does not mean it. All three of the card's examples are todavía no, which had no line of its own.

delea1/salir.why: 'to go out, to leave, to depart, to head out' and then 'to go out' again - four words, then a repeat. salir DE, which is the shape the card's own second example takes (sale de casa), and salir con had no line.

to come out, to turn out

delea1/el hermano, la hermana.why: 'brother' and 'sibling', so SISTER was missing from a card that is a pair - the third such card in the deck after el hijo, la hija and el chico, la chica. dropEx: La niña tomó la mano de su madre.

delea1/el lado.why: 'side' and 'face', the second being the geometer's sense. al lado de, which is how Spanish says 'next to', has no other home in the deck. Its first and third examples are also the same sentence twice - somebody did not see somebody por ningún lado - so one makes room.

por ningún lado — anywhere (with a negative)
dropEx: Tom no vio a Mary por ningún lado.

The bank is next to the hotel.

delea1/el chico, la chica.why: 'boy, kid, guy, lad' - four words for the masculine and none at all for the feminine, on a card that is a pair. Third time in this deck, after el hijo, la hija and el hermano, la hermana.
senses: los chicos — the kids, the children (of either sex)

delea1/quizá.why: Right, and silent on the variant: quizás is as common as quizá and is the form half the corpus uses. tal vez, which means the same and now sits on the vez card, is worth naming beside it.

delea1/durante.why: 'during, in, over, for (as a duration)' is four prepositions where two will do, and the parenthesis on the last is doing the work the example should.
senses: for (a length of time: durante dos horas)

delea1/rápido, rápida.why: Three synonyms for one adjective, and no mention that rápido is also the adverb - habla muy rápido - which is how it is most often heard.

delea1/cuál.why: Filed as a DETERMINER, and all three of its examples are the pronoun (¿cuál es…?). Careful Spanish does not say ¿cuál libro? - the determiner is qué - so the card's part of speech and its examples disagreed, which is the fourth time in this review after hasta, mañana and demasiado. The plural cuáles, which its own second example bolds, was in no Forms row.
senses: what (¿cuál es tu nombre? — what is your name?)

delea1/la historia.why: Two disambiguated glosses both meaning history, and STORY - which is what TWO of the card's three examples are (muchas historias para contar, la historia completa) - was not there at all.

delea1/casi.why: 'almost' alone; casi nada and casi nunca, which is what the card's third example is, needed a line.
senses: hardly any, hardly ever (casi nada, casi nunca)

delea1/la puerta.why: Two dictionary definitions - 'door (portal of entry into a building)' and 'gate (doorlike structure outside a house)'. Its third example, 'Todo niño se porta mal de vez en cuando', bolds porta, from portarse, to behave: a different verb matched because its letters sit inside the headword's, the same fault as mano inside hermano.
dropEx: Todo niño se porta mal de vez en cuando.

delea1/mil.why: FOUND BY A PROBE FOR A BOLDED WORD THAT IS NOT A FORM OF ITS HEADWORD. examples.py matches a sentence on any inflected form, and the match is not always a word: nine sentences across the deck illustrate a word that merely SHARES LETTERS with the card's, or a related noun that is not a form of the verb at all. dropEx: Miles Davis fue un músico de jazz americano.

delea1/la ama.why: FOUND BY A PROBE FOR A BOLDED WORD THAT IS NOT A FORM OF ITS HEADWORD. examples.py matches a sentence on any inflected form, and the match is not always a word: nine sentences across the deck illustrate a word that merely SHARES LETTERS with the card's, or a related noun that is not a form of the verb at all. Las amas de casa trabajan mucho.

delea1/venir.why: THE WORST GLOSS IN THE DECK: its two bullets were 'Senses relating to literal movement.' and 'Senses relating to figurative movement.' — Wiktionary's own SENSE-GROUP HEADERS, the lines a dictionary prints above a list of meanings, extracted as though they were the meanings. delea1/pasar.why: Its second example is '¿Cómo fue el fin de semana pasada, Nancy?', where pasada does not agree - el fin is masculine, so it is el fin de semana pasado. dropEx: ¿Cómo fue el fin de semana pasada, Nancy?

delea1/primero, primera.why: 'first up' and 'top (head)' are not translations of primero. It's the first time I've come here.

delea1/la semana.why: 'week (7 days)' and nothing else, while el fin de semana is the card's own third example and la semana que viene and la semana pasada are how the word is met in a diary. That third example is also the ungrammatical 'fin de semana pasada' the pasar card carried.

la semana que viene — next week

delea1/el año.why: 'year' and 'age' - and año does not mean age; what it does is carry it, in tener … años, which the tener card now states and this one did not. el año pasado and el año que viene are the two phrases the word is met in.
senses: tener … años — to be … years old
el año que viene — next year

delea1/el tío, la tía.why: 'uncle' and 'mister (title conferred on an adult male)', so AUNT was missing from a pair card - the fourth in this deck after el hijo la hija, el hermano la hermana and el chico la chica. delea1/la ciudad.why: Glossed 'city' while two of its three examples translate it 'town' and one of them contrasts it with pueblos.
senses: el centro de la ciudad — the town centre

delea1/cuánto.why: Filed as an ADVERB, with no Forms, while two of its three examples bold cuántas and cuántos - the determiner agreeing with a noun. senses: how much (¿cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost?)

delea1/el jefe, la jefa.why: 'chief, president, head, leader of a business, political party, or other organization' - four glosses, the last a definition, and BOSS, the ordinary English word, among none of them, though the card's own second example is translated 'The boss of the company'.
senses: head, chief (el jefe de cocina — the head chef)

delea1/el agua.why: This is the deck's canonical stressed-a noun - the one the article card names when it says a feminine noun beginning with a stressed a- takes el in the singular - and its own card said nothing about it. senses: las aguas — waters (of a sea or a river)
forms: feminine, but takes el in the singular

delea1/gordo, gorda.why: FOUND BY A SWEEP FOR EXAMPLES A READER SHOULD NOT BE SHOWN. Nothing in the pipeline looks at what an example SAYS, only at whether it contains the word. senses: thick (un libro gordo — a thick book)
el gordo — the jackpot (in the Spanish lottery)
dropEx: Yo no sé por qué Tom es gordo.
Esa chica de allí está muy gorda.
Muy pocos hombres gordos tienen narices largas.
ex: I bought a very thick book.
A mi abuela le tocó el gordo.

delea1/feo, fea.why: FOUND BY A SWEEP FOR EXAMPLES A READER SHOULD NOT BE SHOWN. The sentences come from Tatoeba, which is not written for a classroom, and three cards were carrying sentences that are crude or unkind about a person. Nothing in the pipeline looks at what an example SAYS, only at whether it contains the word. Two of this card's three examples were insults about a person's looks, one of them about a named girl's face. The third is the figurative sense - things turning ugly - which is worth keeping and was the card's own second gloss, written as 'in poor condition'.
senses: nasty, bad (un tiempo feo — bad weather; ponerse feo — to turn nasty)
